topic.title: Two Pointers
topic.summary: Walk two indices through an array or string so each step rules out work a nested loop would repeat — turning O(n²) pair searches into O(n) passes with O(1) memory.
topic.overview:
**Two pointers** means keeping two indices into the same sequence (or one in each of two sequences) and moving them by a rule, so that every move rules out work a nested loop would have repeated. It typically turns an O(n²) pair search into an O(n) pass with O(1) extra memory — exactly the improvement interviewers want you to reason about out loud.

### Three shapes to recognise
1. **Opposite ends (converging)** — `left = 0`, `right = n − 1`, moving toward each other. You need a rule that says which side to move: sorted order (pair sums, 3Sum), symmetry (palindromes) or a limiting side (container, rain water).
2. **Read / write (same direction)** — a fast `read` pointer visits every element; a slow `write` pointer marks where the next kept element goes. Used for in-place filtering: remove duplicates, move zeroes.
3. **Partition / merge** — several pointers carve the array into regions (Dutch national flag) or merge two sorted sequences (merge sorted array, from the back).

### What interviewers listen for
- The brute force first, then **why a pointer move is safe** ("with the largest value available the sum is still too small, so this value can never be in the answer").
- The **loop invariant** ("`nums[0..write−1]` holds the answer so far").
- Off-by-one care: `left < right` vs `left <= right`, empty and single-element input.

### How to study this topic
Work through the questions in order. Valid Palindrome and Two Sum II teach converging pointers; 3Sum adds an outer loop and duplicate skipping; Container and Trapping Rain Water teach "move the limiting side"; the last four rewrite arrays in place. For each one, say the invariant before you write code, then step through the visual to check yourself.

cheatsheet.title: Signals that two pointers fit
points: The input is sorted, or can be sorted without losing what you must return
You need a pair or triplet with a target sum
The array must be changed in place with O(1) extra space
You compare mirrored positions (palindromes)

cheatsheet.title: Converging pointers
points: Loop while left < right
Move the pointer whose move can still improve the answer
Each move discards a whole row/column of pairs → O(n)
Sum too small → left++; too big → right--

cheatsheet.title: Read / write pointers
points: read visits everything; write advances only when you keep a value
Invariant: nums[0..write−1] is the result so far
write ≤ read, so you never overwrite unread data
Return write as the new length

cheatsheet.title: Complexities to quote
points: Pair search on a sorted array: O(n) time, O(1) space
3Sum: O(n²) time after an O(n log n) sort
In-place filters and partitions: O(n) time, O(1) space
Merge two sorted arrays: O(m + n)

cheatsheet.title: Classic traps
points: 3Sum: skip duplicates by comparing with the previous element, not the next
Merging from the front overwrites unread values
Dutch flag: do not advance mid after swapping with high
Rain water: settle the lower side, not the taller one

patterns.name: Opposite ends (converging)
patterns.whenToUse: Sorted arrays (pair/triplet sums), palindromes, "pick two ends" problems where one side is clearly the limit.

patterns.name: Read / write (fast & slow)
patterns.whenToUse: Filter or compact an array in place while keeping order: remove duplicates, remove a value, move zeroes.

patterns.name: Three-way partition (Dutch national flag)
patterns.whenToUse: Group values into < / = / > a pivot (or three categories) in one pass.

patterns.name: Merge from the back
patterns.whenToUse: Merge two sorted sequences into the one that has spare room at its end.

questions.title: Valid Palindrome
questions.prompt:
Given a string `s`, return `true` if it reads the same forwards and backwards **after** lowercasing every letter and removing every character that is not a letter or a digit. Otherwise return `false`.

If nothing is left after cleaning, the (empty) string counts as a palindrome.

examples.explanation: Cleaned: "racecar", which is the same reversed.
Cleaned: "sittie" — its first and last characters ("s" and "e") already differ.
Nothing is left after cleaning, and the empty string is a palindrome.

hints: A palindrome mirrors around its centre: the first character must equal the last, the second the second-to-last, and so on.
Can you compare those mirrored pairs without building a new, cleaned string?
Put `left` at the start and `right` at the end. Skip a non-alphanumeric character on either side, compare lowercase forms, and move both pointers inward on a match.

approaches.name: Clean, then reverse
approaches.idea: Build a lowercase string of only letters/digits and compare it with its reverse.

approaches.name: Clean, then two pointers
approaches.idea: Build the cleaned string, then compare it from both ends. Saves the reversed copy but still allocates.

approaches.name: Two pointers in place
approaches.idea: Skip invalid characters on the fly and compare `s[left]` with `s[right]` directly.

solution.summary: Walk two pointers in from both ends, skip anything that is not a letter or digit, and compare the lowercase characters; the first mismatch means false, and if the pointers meet it is a palindrome. O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
solution.explanation:
**Intuition.** A palindrome is symmetric, so only mirrored pairs need checking: `s[0]` with `s[n−1]`, `s[1]` with `s[n−2]`, and so on. The twist is that spaces and punctuation are ignored and case does not matter.

**Algorithm**
1. `left = 0`, `right = n − 1`.
2. While `left < right`:
   - `s[left]` is not a letter/digit → `left++` (and loop again);
   - else `s[right]` is not a letter/digit → `right--`;
   - else the lowercase forms differ → return `false`;
   - else (a matching pair) → `left++`, `right--`.
3. Return `true`.

**Why it is correct.** Every iteration either throws away a character that the cleaned string would not contain, or verifies one mirrored pair of the cleaned string. When the pointers meet or cross, every pair has been verified. The middle character of an odd-length string has no partner, which is why the condition is `left < right`, not `<=`.

**Edge cases**
- Only punctuation (`" ,."`) → the pointers skip until they cross → `true`.
- Digits count: `"0P"` compares `'0'` with `'p'` → `false`.
- Unicode: Python's `isalnum()` and Java's `Character.isLetterOrDigit()` also accept letters like `é`; the JavaScript regex only accepts ASCII. The problem promises ASCII, but say this if asked.

complexity.time: O(n) — each character is visited at most once by one of the pointers
complexity.space: O(1) — only two indices, no cleaned copy

keyPoints: Compare mirrored pairs from both ends instead of building a reversed copy
Skip non-alphanumeric characters inside the loop, one pointer at a time
Compare lowercase forms so "R" matches "r"; digits are valid characters
`left < right` is enough — the middle character of an odd-length string needs no partner
O(n) time and O(1) space, versus O(n) space for clean-and-reverse

visuals.title: Two pointers on s = "Race, car"
visuals.caption: Yellow = the pair being compared, blue = pairs already matched, red/grey = characters ignored (␣ is a space).

steps.note: Start with `left = 0` and `right = 8`. We compare characters from the outside in and ignore anything that is not a letter or digit.
'R' and 'r' match after lowercasing, so this mirrored pair is fine. Move both pointers inward.
'a' and 'a' match, so this mirrored pair is fine. Move both pointers inward.
'c' and 'c' match, so this mirrored pair is fine. Move both pointers inward.
`s[right]` is a space, not a letter or digit, so it is ignored: `right--`. `left` waits where it is.
`s[right]` is ',' (punctuation), not a letter or digit, so it is ignored: `right--`. `left` waits where it is.
`left` (3) is no longer < `right` (3): the pointers met at 'e', the middle character, which needs no partner. Every pair matched → return **true** ("racecar" is a palindrome).

visuals.title: Clean-and-reverse vs in-place two pointers
rows: Build a lowercase letters/digits copy, compare it with its reverse
Compare s[left] and s[right], skipping invalid characters on the fly
O(n) — the cleaned copy (and its reverse)
No — the whole copy is built before comparing
Yes — stops at the first mismatched pair
When the interviewer asks to avoid extra memory

pitfalls: Skipping with an inner `while` that does not re-check `left < right`, so a pointer runs past the other one (or off the string)
Forgetting that digits are valid characters
Comparing before lowercasing, so "A" vs "a" looks like a mismatch
Calling `cleaned.split("").reverse().join("")` an O(1)-space solution

followUps.question: What if you may delete at most one character?
followUps.answer: Run the same loop; on the first mismatch try both options — skip `s[left]` or skip `s[right]` — and check whether either remaining range is a palindrome with a plain two-pointer check. Still O(n).

followUps.question: How would you support full Unicode?
followUps.answer: Use Unicode-aware checks (`/[\p{L}\p{N}]/u` in JavaScript, `Character.isLetterOrDigit(int codePoint)` in Java), iterate by code point, and normalise the string (e.g. NFC) first, because one visible character can be several code units.

questions.title: Two Sum II — Input Array Is Sorted
questions.prompt:
You are given an array `numbers` that is already **sorted in non-decreasing order**, and an integer `target`. Exactly one pair of different positions adds up to `target`.

Return the two positions as **1-based** indices `[index1, index2]` with `index1 < index2`, using only O(1) extra space.

examples.explanation: 4 + 6 = 10; they sit at 0-based indices 2 and 3, i.e. 1-based [3, 4].

hints: The array is sorted. What does that tell you about the sum of the smallest and the largest value?
If `numbers[left] + numbers[right]` is too small, can `numbers[left]` reach the target with any other partner?
Start with `left = 0`, `right = n − 1`. Sum too small → `left++`; too big → `right--`; equal → done.

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: Check every pair (i, j).

approaches.name: Binary search per element
approaches.idea: For each i, binary-search `target − numbers[i]` to its right.

approaches.name: Hash map
approaches.idea: One pass with a value → index map, as in unsorted Two Sum. Ignores the sorted order and uses memory.

approaches.name: Two pointers
approaches.idea: Start at both ends and move the pointer that can fix the sum.

solution.summary: Because the array is sorted, I put one pointer at each end: if the sum is too small I move the left pointer right, if it is too big I move the right pointer left, and I stop when it equals the target. Each move safely discards one value, so it is O(n) time and O(1) space.
solution.explanation:
**Intuition.** In a sorted array the smallest value is on the far left and the largest on the far right. Compare `numbers[left] + numbers[right]` with `target`:

- **sum < target** — `numbers[left]` paired with the *largest* value still available is too small, so it cannot be in any answer. Discard it: `left++`.
- **sum > target** — `numbers[right]` paired with the *smallest* value still available is too big. Discard it: `right--`.
- **sum == target** — return `[left + 1, right + 1]` (the problem uses 1-based positions).

**Why the answer is never skipped.** Each move removes a value that provably cannot pair with anything still inside `[left, right]`. The answer pair therefore stays inside the window until the pointers land on it. The second visual shows the "pair table": every move crosses out a whole row or column of sums at once.

**Complexity.** Each iteration moves one pointer one step, so at most n − 1 iterations: O(n) time, O(1) extra space.

**Edge cases.** Duplicates are fine (`[5, 5]` → `[1, 2]`), and negative numbers are fine because only the order matters. In Java, two large ints could overflow when added — not with these constraints, but worth saying.

complexity.time: O(n) — every step moves one pointer inward, at most n − 1 steps

keyPoints: Sorted input is the signal for converging two pointers
Too small → move left; too big → move right; each move discards a value for good
O(n) time and O(1) space — beats the hash map, which needs O(n) memory
Return 1-based indices
Justify correctness with the "eliminate a row or column of pairs" argument

visuals.title: Two pointers on numbers = [1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 11], target = 10
visuals.caption: Yellow = the pair being summed, grey = values already ruled out, green = the answer.

steps.note: The array is sorted, so `left = 0` sits on the smallest value and `right = 5` on the largest. Their sum tells us which side to move.
1 + 11 = 12 > 10. Even with the smallest value still available, 11 overshoots — discard it: `right--`.
1 + 8 = 9 < 10. Even with the largest value still available, 1 is too small to reach the target — discard it: `left++`.
3 + 8 = 11 > 10. Even with the smallest value still available, 8 overshoots — discard it: `right--`.
3 + 6 = 9 < 10. Even with the largest value still available, 3 is too small to reach the target — discard it: `left++`.
4 + 6 = 10 = target → return the **1-based** positions **[3, 4]**.

visuals.title: Why it is safe: each move eliminates a row or a column of pairs
visuals.caption: Cell (row left, column right) = numbers[left] + numbers[right]. Red = ruled out by this move, grey = ruled out earlier, yellow = the pair being checked.

steps.note: Every cell above the diagonal is one pair (row = left index, column = right index) holding its sum. Brute force checks all 15. Two pointers start in the top-right corner: the smallest value paired with the largest.
Sum 12 > 10. Column 5 grows downward, and this is its smallest remaining sum — so the whole column (red) is too big. Discard it: `right--`.
Sum 9 < 10. Row 0 is sorted left to right, and this is its largest remaining sum — so the whole row (red) is too small. Discard it: `left++`.
Sum 11 > 10. Column 4 grows downward, and this is its smallest remaining sum — so the whole column (red) is too big. Discard it: `right--`.
Sum 9 < 10. Row 1 is sorted left to right, and this is its largest remaining sum — so the whole row (red) is too small. Discard it: `left++`.
Sum 10 = target at (2, 3) → return [3, 4]. The pointers inspected 5 of the 15 pairs; every grey pair was ruled out in bulk, which is why the scan is O(n) instead of O(n²).

pitfalls: Returning 0-based indices when the problem asks for 1-based ones
Using `left <= right`, which can pair an element with itself
Reaching for a hash map and ignoring the sorted order — the interviewer wants O(1) space here

followUps.question: How would you count all pairs with sum ≤ target?
followUps.answer: Same pointers: if `numbers[left] + numbers[right] ≤ target`, then `left` pairs with every index in `(left, right]`, so add `right − left` and move `left`; otherwise move `right`. O(n).

followUps.question: What if the array is not sorted?
followUps.answer: Either use the hash-map Two Sum (O(n) time, O(n) space), or sort (value, index) pairs first (O(n log n)) so the original indices survive.

questions.title: 3Sum
questions.prompt:
Given an integer array `nums`, return **all unique triplets** `[a, b, c]` taken from three different positions such that `a + b + c == 0`.

The result must not contain the same triplet twice (as a multiset of values). The order of the triplets, and of the values inside each triplet, does not matter.

examples.explanation: -2 appears twice, but [-2, 0, 2] is listed only once.

hints: If you fix the first number `a`, what problem is left on the remaining numbers?
Two Sum on a sorted array takes O(n) with two pointers — and sorting also puts duplicates next to each other.
Sort; for each index i run two pointers on `(i, n − 1)` looking for `−nums[i]`. Skip an anchor equal to the previous one, and after a match move `left` past equal values.

approaches.name: Brute force + set
approaches.idea: Three nested loops; store each sorted triplet in a set to remove duplicates.
approaches.space: O(k) for the set of k triplets

approaches.name: Hash set per anchor
approaches.idea: Fix i, then run a hash-set Two Sum for `−nums[i]` on the rest; dedupe with a set of sorted triplets.

approaches.name: Sort + two pointers
approaches.idea: Sort, fix each anchor, run two pointers on the rest and skip equal neighbours.
approaches.space: O(1) besides the sort and the output

solution.summary: Sort the array, fix each number as the first element, and solve Two Sum for its negative on the part to its right with two pointers. Skipping equal anchors, and equal left values after a match, removes duplicate triplets without a hash set. O(n²) time, O(1) extra space besides sorting.
solution.explanation:
**Reduce to a problem you know.** `a + b + c = 0` means `b + c = −a`. Fix `a = nums[i]`, and finding `b, c` is *Two Sum on a sorted array* — two pointers in O(n).

**Algorithm**
1. Sort `nums`. This gives the two-pointer property and groups equal values.
2. For each anchor index `i`:
   - If `nums[i] > 0`, **stop**: the anchor is the smallest of the three, so all three would be positive.
   - If `nums[i] == nums[i − 1]`, **skip**: the previous equal anchor already produced every triplet this one could.
   - `left = i + 1`, `right = n − 1`; sum < 0 → `left++`, sum > 0 → `right--`.
   - Sum == 0 → record the triplet, move both pointers, then advance `left` past values equal to the one just used.
3. Return the collected triplets.

**Why there are no duplicates.** A triplet is identified by its sorted values `(a, b, c)`. Skipping equal anchors uses each `a` once; skipping equal `left` values after a match uses each `b` once per `a`; and `c = −a − b` is then forced. So every value-triplet is emitted exactly once.

**Why the anchor check compares with `i − 1`.** It processes the *first* copy of a value while later copies are still available as `b` or `c` — that is how `[-2, 0, 2]` and also `[-1, -1, 2]`-style triplets survive.

**Complexity.** O(n log n) to sort + n anchors × O(n) scan = **O(n²)**.

complexity.time: O(n²) — n anchors, each followed by an O(n) two-pointer scan (sorting is O(n log n))
complexity.space: O(1) extra besides the sort and the output list

keyPoints: Reduce 3Sum to n runs of sorted Two Sum with two pointers
Sort first: it enables pointer moves and groups duplicates
Skip a duplicate anchor (compare with i − 1) and duplicate left values after a match
Early break when the anchor is positive
O(n²) is the expected answer; brute force is O(n³)

visuals.title: Sort + two pointers on nums = [-2, 0, 1, 1, 2, -1, -2]
visuals.caption: `i` is the anchor; `left`/`right` run Two Sum on the rest. Grey cells are finished anchors, green = a triplet was recorded.

steps.note: Sort first: [-2, 0, 1, 1, 2, -1, -2] → [-2, -2, -1, 0, 1, 1, 2]. Sorted order lets us steer the pointers by the sum and puts equal values next to each other, which makes skipping duplicates easy.
Anchor -2: -2 + (-2) + 2 = -2 < 0 → need a bigger sum: `left++`.
Anchor -2: -2 + (-1) + 2 = -1 < 0 → need a bigger sum: `left++`.
Anchor -2: -2 + 0 + 2 = 0 → **record [-2, 0, 2]**. Move both pointers inward → left = 4, right = 5.
Anchor -2: -2 + 1 + 1 = 0 → **record [-2, 1, 1]**. Move both pointers inward → they cross, so this anchor is done.
`nums[1]` = -2 equals the previous anchor. Every triplet starting with -2 was already found, so **skip** this anchor.
Anchor -1: -1 + 0 + 2 = 1 > 0 → need a smaller sum: `right--`.
Anchor -1: -1 + 0 + 1 = 0 → **record [-1, 0, 1]**. Move both pointers inward → they meet (left = right = 4), so this anchor is done.
Anchor 0: 0 + 1 + 2 = 3 > 0 → need a smaller sum: `right--`.
Anchor 0: 0 + 1 + 1 = 2 > 0 → need a smaller sum: `right--`.
`nums[i]` = 1 > 0. Everything from here on is positive, so no triplet can sum to 0 — **break**.
Done: 3 unique triplets (green = positions used by a recorded triplet; the duplicate anchor at index 1 was skipped), found with O(n²) pointer moves and no hash set.

visuals.title: Three ways to find all zero-sum triplets
rows: Fix i, hash-set Two Sum on the rest
Sort, fix i, two pointers on the rest
O(n) set per anchor + result set
Skip equal neighbours — no set needed
Say it as the baseline only

pitfalls: Skipping when `nums[i] == nums[i + 1]` instead of `nums[i − 1]` — the first copy is skipped and triplets like [-1, -1, 2] are lost
Forgetting to move the pointers after recording a match, which loops forever
Deduping with a JavaScript `Set` of arrays — arrays compare by reference, so duplicates stay
Returning indices instead of values

followUps.question: How would you solve 3Sum Closest (sum closest to a target)?
followUps.answer: Same sort + two pointers; track the sum with the smallest |sum − target| and move the pointers by comparing the sum with the target. O(n²).

followUps.question: And 4Sum?
followUps.answer: Add another outer loop (two fixed anchors) with the same duplicate skipping: O(n³). In general k-Sum costs O(n^(k−1)).

followUps.question: Can 3Sum be done faster than O(n²)?
followUps.answer: Not meaningfully — it is widely believed that no O(n^(2−ε)) algorithm exists (the "3SUM conjecture"); only tiny log-factor improvements are known. O(n²) is what interviewers expect.

questions.title: Container With Most Water
questions.prompt:
You are given an array `height` of n non-negative integers. `height[i]` is a vertical wall standing at x = i.

Pick two walls. Together with the x-axis they form a container whose water level is capped by the **shorter** wall, so it holds `min(height[i], height[j]) × (j − i)` units.

Return the maximum amount of water a single container can hold. (Walls between the two chosen ones are ignored, and the container cannot be tilted.)
hints: The amount of water depends only on the width and on the shorter of the two walls.
Start with the widest container. Any inward move makes it narrower — which move could possibly make it hold more?
Always move the pointer at the shorter wall. Keeping the shorter wall with a closer partner can never do better.

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: Compute the area for every pair of walls.

approaches.name: Two pointers (greedy)
approaches.idea: Start at both ends, record the area, then move the shorter wall inward.

solution.summary: Start with the widest container, one pointer at each end, record its area, then move the pointer at the shorter wall inward — the shorter wall caps the height, so pairing it with any closer wall can only lose width. One pass: O(n) time, O(1) space.
solution.explanation:
**Area.** `area(i, j) = min(height[i], height[j]) × (j − i)`: the shorter wall sets the height, the distance sets the width.

**The greedy step.** Start with `left = 0`, `right = n − 1` (maximum width). Suppose `height[left] < height[right]`. Any other container that keeps `left` uses a partner `j < right`, so:
- its width is smaller than `right − left`, and
- its height is at most `height[left]`.

So every container that still uses `left` is no better than the one just measured → discard `left` for good: `left++`. Symmetrically, if `height[right] ≤ height[left]`, discard `right`. On a tie either move is safe, because both walls are then "the shorter one".

**Algorithm**
1. `best = 0`.
2. While `left < right`: compute the area, update `best`, move the pointer at the shorter wall.
3. Return `best`.

**Complexity.** n − 1 iterations → O(n) time, O(1) space. The grid visual is the proof: each move crosses out a whole row or column of pairs whose area cannot beat one we have already measured.

complexity.time: O(n) — each iteration discards one wall

keyPoints: Area = min(height) × width — the shorter wall is the limit
Start at maximum width, then always move the shorter wall
Proof: keeping the shorter wall with a narrower partner can never increase the area
O(n) time, O(1) space versus O(n²) brute force

visuals.title: Two pointers on height = [2, 7, 3, 6, 4, 8, 1, 5]
visuals.caption: The band is the current container. Grey walls have been discarded for good; green = the best pair.

steps.note: Start with the widest container: `left = 0`, `right = 7`, `best = 0`.
Area = min(2, 5) × 7 = 14 → **new best 14**. height[left] = 2 is the shorter wall, so every narrower container that keeps it is worse — discard it: `left++`.
Area = min(7, 5) × 6 = 30 → **new best 30**. height[right] = 5 is the shorter wall, so discard it: `right--`.
Area = min(7, 1) × 5 = 5 (best stays 30). height[right] = 1 is the shorter wall, so discard it: `right--`.
Area = min(7, 8) × 4 = 28 (best stays 30). height[left] = 7 is the shorter wall, so every narrower container that keeps it is worse — discard it: `left++`.
Area = min(3, 8) × 3 = 9 (best stays 30). height[left] = 3 is the shorter wall, so every narrower container that keeps it is worse — discard it: `left++`.
Area = min(6, 8) × 2 = 12 (best stays 30). height[left] = 6 is the shorter wall, so every narrower container that keeps it is worse — discard it: `left++`.
Area = min(4, 8) × 1 = 4 (best stays 30). height[left] = 4 is the shorter wall, so every narrower container that keeps it is worse — discard it: `left++`.
`left` meets `right`: return **30**, from the walls at index 1 (height 7) and 7 (height 5).

visuals.title: Each move rules out a whole row or column of pairs
visuals.caption: Cell (row i, column j) = area of walls i and j. Yellow = measured now, red = ruled out by this move, grey = ruled out earlier, green = best.

steps.note: Cell (row i, column j) is the area of walls i and j. Brute force computes all 28. Two pointers start at the widest pair (0, 7), the top-right corner.
Area(0, 7) = 14 (new best). Wall 0 (height 2) is shorter: any pair (0, j) with j < 7 is narrower and still at most 2 high, so the whole row (red) can't win. `left++`.
Area(1, 7) = 30 (new best). Wall 7 (height 5) is the shorter (or equal) one: any pair (i, 7) with i > 1 is narrower and at most 5 high, so the whole column (red) can't win. `right--`.
Area(1, 6) = 5. Wall 6 (height 1) is the shorter (or equal) one: any pair (i, 6) with i > 1 is narrower and at most 1 high, so the whole column (red) can't win. `right--`.
Area(1, 5) = 28. Wall 1 (height 7) is shorter: any pair (1, j) with j < 5 is narrower and still at most 7 high, so the whole row (red) can't win. `left++`.
Area(2, 5) = 9. Wall 2 (height 3) is shorter: any pair (2, j) with j < 5 is narrower and still at most 3 high, so the whole row (red) can't win. `left++`.
Area(3, 5) = 12. Wall 3 (height 6) is shorter: any pair (3, j) with j < 5 is narrower and still at most 6 high, so the whole row (red) can't win. `left++`.
Area(4, 5) = 4. Wall 4 (height 4) is shorter: any pair (4, j) with j < 5 is narrower and still at most 4 high, so the whole row (red) can't win. `left++`.
All 28 pairs are ruled out after measuring only 7 of them. The best one, (1, 7) with area 30, was measured along the way — greedy pruning never discarded it.

pitfalls: Moving the taller wall — it can never help and may skip the optimum
Confusing this with Trapping Rain Water (that sums water above every bar)
Multiplying by the taller wall instead of the shorter one

followUps.question: Why is moving either pointer on a tie safe?
followUps.answer: With equal heights h, any container that keeps either wall with a closer partner is narrower and at most h high, so neither wall can beat the current area; discarding either is safe.

followUps.question: How is this different from Trapping Rain Water?
followUps.answer: Here you choose two walls and ignore everything between them. In rain water every gap fills, so you add up the water above each bar using the tallest walls on its left and right.

questions.title: Trapping Rain Water
questions.prompt:
`height[i]` is the height of a bar of width 1 in an elevation map. After it rains, water collects in the dips between bars.

Return the total number of units of water that stay trapped.

examples.explanation: 3 + 1 + 3 units above the three inner bars.
The heights only go down, so the water runs off.

hints: Think about one index at a time: how high can water stand above bar i?
Water above i = min(tallest bar on its left, tallest bar on its right) − height[i], counting bar i itself on both sides.
Prefix and suffix max arrays give O(n) time with O(n) space. For O(1) space, walk two pointers inward from the lower side — that side's running max is the limit.

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: For every index, scan left and right for the tallest bars.

approaches.name: Prefix and suffix maxima
approaches.idea: Precompute leftMax[i] and rightMax[i], then add min(leftMax, rightMax) − height.

approaches.name: Monotonic stack
approaches.idea: Keep a stack of indices with decreasing heights; a taller bar pops a "floor" and adds the layer of water above it.

approaches.name: Two pointers
approaches.idea: Move inward from the lower side, tracking leftMax and rightMax.

solution.summary: Water above each bar is min(tallest bar on its left, tallest bar on its right) minus its own height. With two pointers I always process the lower side: that side's running max is guaranteed to be the limiting wall, so I can add its water immediately. O(n) time, O(1) space.
solution.explanation:
**Per-bar formula.**

`water[i] = min(maxLeft(i), maxRight(i)) − height[i]`

where `maxLeft(i)` is the tallest bar in `[0..i]` and `maxRight(i)` the tallest in `[i..n−1]` (including bar i, so the result is never negative). The second visual computes both arrays — a correct O(n)-space answer and a good first thing to say.

**Dropping the arrays with two pointers.** Keep `left`, `right`, `leftMax` (tallest seen from the left) and `rightMax` (tallest seen from the right).
- If `height[left] < height[right]`: the right side already contains a bar taller than `height[left]`, and every bar the left pointer has passed was lower than some bar on the right (that is why it was passed). So the true `maxRight(left)` is at least `leftMax`, which makes **leftMax the limit**: add `leftMax − height[left]` (after updating leftMax) and move `left` right.
- Otherwise the mirror argument holds: add `rightMax − height[right]` and move `right` left.

**Complexity.** Every index is settled exactly once → O(n) time, O(1) extra space.

**Edge cases.** Fewer than 3 bars cannot trap water. Monotonic heights trap 0. The pointers meet at a tallest bar, which holds no water.

code.code:
def trap(height):
    left, right = 0, len(height) - 1
    left_max = right_max = 0
    water = 0
    while left < right:
        if height[left] < height[right]:
            left_max = max(left_max, height[left])
            water += left_max - height[left]
            left += 1
        else:
            right_max = max(right_max, height[right])
            water += right_max - height[right]
            right -= 1
    return water

complexity.time: O(n) — each index is settled once
complexity.space: O(1) — four variables instead of two helper arrays

keyPoints: State the per-bar formula: min(maxLeft, maxRight) − height[i]
Prefix/suffix max arrays: O(n) time, O(n) space — a solid first answer
Two pointers: settle the lower side, because its running max is the bottleneck
O(n) time, O(1) space; mention the monotonic-stack alternative

visuals.title: Two pointers on height = [3, 0, 2, 0, 4, 1, 0, 2]
visuals.caption: The second row fills in the water above each bar as it is settled. Blue = settled, highlighted = settled in this step.

steps.note: Pointers at both ends, `leftMax = rightMax = 0`, `water = 0`. Each step settles the bar on the **lower** side.
height[left] = 3 ≥ height[right] = 2: the left side has a wall at least as tall as rightMax, so rightMax decides. rightMax = 2, water above index 7 = 2 − 2 = **0**. Then `right--`.
height[left] = 3 ≥ height[right] = 0: the left side has a wall at least as tall as rightMax, so rightMax decides. rightMax = 2, water above index 6 = 2 − 0 = **2**. Then `right--`.
height[left] = 3 ≥ height[right] = 1: the left side has a wall at least as tall as rightMax, so rightMax decides. rightMax = 2, water above index 5 = 2 − 1 = **1**. Then `right--`.
height[left] = 3 < height[right] = 4: the right side has a wall at least as tall as leftMax, so leftMax decides. leftMax = 3, water above index 0 = 3 − 3 = **0**. Then `left++`.
height[left] = 0 < height[right] = 4: the right side has a wall at least as tall as leftMax, so leftMax decides. leftMax = 3, water above index 1 = 3 − 0 = **3**. Then `left++`.
height[left] = 2 < height[right] = 4: the right side has a wall at least as tall as leftMax, so leftMax decides. leftMax = 3, water above index 2 = 3 − 2 = **1**. Then `left++`.
height[left] = 0 < height[right] = 4: the right side has a wall at least as tall as leftMax, so leftMax decides. leftMax = 3, water above index 3 = 3 − 0 = **3**. Then `left++`.
`left` meets `right` at index 4, the tallest bar (no water above it). Total trapped water = **10**.

visuals.title: The O(n)-space version: prefix and suffix maxima
visuals.caption: Rows: height, leftMax, rightMax, water. water[i] = min(leftMax[i], rightMax[i]) − height[i].

steps.note: Water above bar i depends on the tallest bar to its left and the tallest bar to its right. Compute both for every index first.
Left to right: `leftMax[i] = max(leftMax[i − 1], height[i])` → [3, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 4].
Right to left: `rightMax[i] = max(rightMax[i + 1], height[i])` → [4, 4, 4, 4, 4, 2, 2, 2].
For each column the **smaller** of the two maxima (yellow) is the wall the water spills over: `water[i] = min(leftMax[i], rightMax[i]) − height[i]`.
Sum of the last row = **10**. Same answer as two pointers, but with O(n) extra arrays. Notice only the smaller maximum matters — that is why two pointers can drop the arrays.

pitfalls: Using max instead of min of the two sides
Subtracting before updating `leftMax`/`rightMax`, which can produce negative water
Settling the taller side — its running max is not guaranteed to be the limit
Confusing it with Container With Most Water, which picks only two walls

followUps.question: How does the monotonic-stack solution work?
followUps.answer: Keep indices with decreasing heights. When `height[i]` is taller than the top, pop it as the floor; the new top is the left wall and i the right wall, so add `(min(height[left], height[i]) − height[floor]) × (i − left − 1)`. Each index is pushed and popped once: O(n).

followUps.question: What about a 2-D elevation map?
followUps.answer: Use a min-heap seeded with every border cell and grow inward from the lowest boundary cell (like Dijkstra); a neighbour lower than the current boundary traps the difference. O(mn log(mn)).

questions.title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array
questions.prompt:
Given an integer array `nums` sorted in non-decreasing order, remove the duplicates **in place** so that each distinct value appears once, keeping the original order.

Return `k`, the number of distinct values. The first `k` slots of `nums` must hold those values; whatever is left after index `k − 1` does not matter. Use O(1) extra memory.

examples.explanation: "_" means any value — the caller only reads the first k slots.

hints: Because the array is sorted, all copies of a value sit next to each other.
Use one pointer to read every element and another to mark where the next distinct value should be written.
Compare `nums[read]` with the last value you kept, `nums[write − 1]`; if it differs, copy it to `nums[write]` and advance `write`.

approaches.name: Extra set or array
approaches.idea: Collect distinct values in a new structure, then copy them back.

approaches.name: Shift on every duplicate
approaches.idea: When a duplicate is found, shift the rest of the array one step left.

approaches.name: Read / write pointers
approaches.idea: A fast `read` pointer scans; a slow `write` pointer overwrites in place.

solution.summary: Use a slow `write` pointer and a fast `read` pointer. Because the array is sorted, a value is new exactly when it differs from the last kept value `nums[write − 1]`, so I copy it to `nums[write]` and advance. Return `write`. One pass, O(1) space.
solution.explanation:
**Invariant.** `nums[0..write−1]` always holds the distinct values seen so far, in order.

**Algorithm**
1. Empty array → return 0. The first element is always kept, so `write = 1`.
2. For `read` from 1 to n − 1:
   - `nums[read] != nums[write − 1]` → a new value: `nums[write] = nums[read]`, `write++`;
   - otherwise it is a copy of the last kept value: skip it.
3. Return `write`.

**Why it is correct.** Sorted order puts all copies of a value next to each other, so comparing with the *last kept* value is enough to recognise a new one. `write ≤ read` always holds, so a write never destroys an element that still has to be read.

**Complexity.** One pass: O(n) time, O(1) extra space. Slots after `k − 1` keep leftover values — the caller ignores them, and an in-place algorithm cannot shrink a fixed-size array anyway.

complexity.time: O(n) — one pass with the read pointer

keyPoints: Read/write (fast/slow) pointers are the standard in-place filter
Invariant: nums[0..write−1] holds the distinct values so far
Compare with the last kept value nums[write − 1]
write never passes read, so nothing unread is overwritten
Comparing with nums[write − k] generalises to "keep at most k copies"

visuals.title: Read/write pointers on nums = [1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 3, 5]
visuals.caption: The band is the kept prefix nums[0..write−1]. Red = duplicate skipped by `read`, highlighted = value just written.

steps.note: nums[0] = 1 is always kept, so `write = 1`. `read` will scan from index 1 and compare each value with the last kept one, `nums[write − 1]`.
nums[read] = 1 equals the last kept value → duplicate, skip it (`write` stays 1).
nums[read] = 2 ≠ last kept 1 → a new value: copy it into nums[1] and `write` becomes 2.
nums[read] = 3 ≠ last kept 2 → a new value: copy it into nums[2] and `write` becomes 3.
nums[read] = 3 equals the last kept value → duplicate, skip it (`write` stays 3).
nums[read] = 3 equals the last kept value → duplicate, skip it (`write` stays 3).
nums[read] = 5 ≠ last kept 3 → a new value: copy it into nums[3] and `write` becomes 4.
`read` reached the end → return **k = 4**. nums[0..3] = [1, 2, 3, 5]; the cells after it are leftovers the caller ignores.

visuals.title: Three ways to deduplicate a sorted array
rows: Collect distinct values elsewhere, copy back
Delete each duplicate by shifting the tail
Overwrite in place using a write index

pitfalls: Returning the array instead of the count k
Starting `write` at 0 and then reading `nums[write − 1]` = nums[−1]
Calling `splice`/`remove` inside the loop — O(n²) and the indices shift under you

followUps.question: Allow each value at most twice?
followUps.answer: Start with `write = 2` and keep `nums[read]` when it differs from `nums[write − 2]`. The same idea works for any limit k.

followUps.question: What if the array is not sorted?
followUps.answer: Copies are no longer adjacent. Use a hash set of seen values (O(n) space) with the same read/write pointers, or sort first if the original order does not matter.

questions.title: Move Zeroes
questions.prompt: Given an integer array `nums`, move every `0` to the end **in place**, keeping the relative order of the non-zero values. Do not make a copy of the array.
hints: Think of it as "keep the non-zero values, in order" — the zeros are just what is left over.
Keep a `write` index: the slot where the next non-zero value should go.
Scan with `read`; whenever `nums[read] != 0`, swap it with `nums[write]` and advance `write`. Swapping (instead of copying) leaves the zeros at the end automatically.

approaches.name: Extra array
approaches.idea: Copy non-zeros into a new array, pad with zeros, copy back.

approaches.name: Copy forward, then zero-fill
approaches.idea: Read/write pointers copy non-zeros forward; a second loop writes zeros into the tail.

approaches.name: Swap in one pass
approaches.idea: Read/write pointers swap each non-zero into place.

solution.summary: Keep a `write` pointer for the next slot of a non-zero value and scan with `read`; whenever `nums[read]` is non-zero I swap it into `nums[write]` and advance `write`. Non-zeros keep their order and the zeros drift to the end — one pass, O(1) space.
solution.explanation:
**Invariant.** After processing `read`, `nums[0..write−1]` holds every non-zero seen so far in its original order, and `nums[write..read]` holds only zeros.

**Algorithm**
1. `write = 0`.
2. For each `read` from 0 to n − 1: if `nums[read] != 0`, swap `nums[write]` with `nums[read]` and `write++`.
3. Nothing to return — the array is modified in place.

**Why swapping works.** Between `write` and `read` there are only zeros (the invariant). The swap moves the new non-zero to the front of that zero block and a zero to its back, so the order of non-zeros is kept and every zero ends up behind the last non-zero.

**Swap vs copy-then-fill.** The two-pass version copies non-zeros forward and then writes zeros into `nums[write..n−1]`. Both are O(n) with O(1) space; the swap version needs a single pass.

**Edge cases.** No zeros → every element swaps with itself (you can skip the swap when `read == write`). All zeros → `write` stays 0 and nothing moves.
keyPoints: Same read/write pointer pattern as removing duplicates
Invariant: non-zeros before write, only zeros between write and read
Swapping keeps the order of the non-zeros and pushes zeros back
O(n) time, O(1) space, single pass

visuals.title: Swap-forward on nums = [4, 0, 0, 7, 0, 3]
visuals.caption: The band holds the non-zeros placed so far; grey cells are the block of zeros between write and read.

steps.note: `write = 0`: the next non-zero value belongs at index 0. `read` visits every index.
nums[0] = 4 is non-zero → swap it with itself (nothing moves); `write` becomes 1.
nums[1] = 0 → leave it. It joins the block of zeros between `write` and `read`.
nums[2] = 0 → leave it. It joins the block of zeros between `write` and `read`.
nums[3] = 7 is non-zero → swap it with the zero at index 1; `write` becomes 2.
nums[4] = 0 → leave it. It joins the block of zeros between `write` and `read`.
nums[5] = 3 is non-zero → swap it with the zero at index 2; `write` becomes 3.
Done: the non-zeros [4, 7, 3] kept their order and all 3 zeros are at the end.

visuals.title: Extra array vs copy-then-fill vs swap

pitfalls: Copying non-zeros forward but forgetting to zero-fill the tail, which leaves stale values behind
Deleting zeros and appending them inside the loop (`splice` + `push`) — O(n²) and the indices shift
Sorting with a "zeros last" comparator: O(n log n) when O(n) is expected

followUps.question: How do you reduce the number of writes?
followUps.answer: Skip the swap when `read == write` (the value is already in place), or copy non-zeros forward and zero-fill only the tail.

followUps.question: Move the zeros to the front instead?
followUps.answer: Mirror it: scan from the right with a write pointer that starts at the last index.

questions.title: Merge Sorted Array
questions.prompt:
You get two arrays sorted in non-decreasing order. `nums1` has length `m + n`: its first `m` values are real and the last `n` slots are placeholders (0). `nums2` holds `n` values.

Merge `nums2` into `nums1` **in place** so that `nums1` becomes one sorted array of length m + n. Return nothing.

examples.explanation: nums1 has no real values; the result is just nums2.

constraints: Both inputs are sorted in non-decreasing order
hints: The free space in nums1 is at the end. Which values belong at the very end of the result?
Merging from the front would overwrite nums1 values you have not read yet. What about from the back?
Use i = m − 1, j = n − 1, k = m + n − 1. Write the larger of nums1[i] and nums2[j] into nums1[k] and step back. Stop when nums2 is used up.

approaches.name: Copy and sort
approaches.idea: Copy nums2 into the tail of nums1 and sort the whole array.
approaches.space: Depends on the sort (O(log n) to O(n))

approaches.name: Merge into a copy
approaches.idea: Standard merge into a new array, then copy it back.

approaches.name: Merge from the back
approaches.idea: Three pointers fill nums1 from its last slot backwards.

solution.summary: Merge from the back: compare the last real value of nums1 with the last value of nums2 and write the larger one into the last free slot, then step that pointer back. Writing from the end never overwrites a value I still need, so it is O(m + n) time and O(1) extra space.
solution.explanation:
**Why not from the front?** The free space in `nums1` is at the end. Writing the smallest value into `nums1[0]` would overwrite a real value that has not been merged yet.

**From the back.** The largest remaining value always belongs in the last unfilled slot.
1. `i = m − 1` (last real value of nums1), `j = n − 1` (last of nums2), `k = m + n − 1` (slot to fill).
2. While `j ≥ 0`:
   - `i ≥ 0` and `nums1[i] > nums2[j]` → `nums1[k] = nums1[i]`, `i--`;
   - otherwise → `nums1[k] = nums2[j]`, `j--`;
   - `k--`.
3. When `j < 0` every nums2 value is placed, and the remaining `nums1[0..i]` values are already where they belong.

**Why nothing is overwritten.** `k = i + j + 1`, so while nums2 still has values (`j ≥ 0`) we have `k > i`: every write lands in a placeholder or in a slot whose value was already moved.

**Complexity.** One value is placed per step: O(m + n) time, O(1) extra space. This is exactly the merge step of merge sort.

complexity.time: O(m + n) — each step places one value

keyPoints: Fill from the back, because that is where the free space is
Loop while nums2 has values; leftover nums1 values are already in place
Check i >= 0 before reading nums1[i]
O(m + n) time, O(1) space — the merge step of merge sort

visuals.title: Merging from the back: nums1 = [2, 5, 8, _, _, _], nums2 = [1, 6, 9]
visuals.caption: `k` is the slot being filled. The band on the right is final; grey nums1 cells are free (placeholders or values already moved).

steps.note: `i = 2` (last real value of nums1), `j = 2` (last of nums2), `k = 5` (last slot). The grey slots in nums1 are free space.
nums1[i] = 8 ≤ nums2[j] = 9 → 9 goes to nums1[5]; `j--`.
nums1[i] = 8 > nums2[j] = 6 → the larger value 8 goes to nums1[4]; `i--`.
nums1[i] = 5 ≤ nums2[j] = 6 → 6 goes to nums1[3]; `j--`.
nums1[i] = 5 > nums2[j] = 1 → the larger value 5 goes to nums1[2]; `i--`.
nums1[i] = 2 > nums2[j] = 1 → the larger value 2 goes to nums1[1]; `i--`.
nums1 has no real values left (`i = −1`) → copy nums2[j] = 1 into nums1[0]; `j--`.
`j < 0`: all of nums2 is placed. Any remaining nums1 values are already in position → nums1 = [1, 2, 5, 6, 8, 9].

visuals.title: Merging from the front vs from the back
rows: nums1[5] = 9 lands in an empty slot
Yes — copy nums1's m values out first
nums2 is consumed (the rest of nums1 is already in place)

pitfalls: Merging from the front and overwriting unread nums1 values
Looping `while (i >= 0 && j >= 0)` and forgetting to copy the rest of nums2
Reading `nums1[i]` when `i = −1`

followUps.question: What if nums1 had no spare capacity?
followUps.answer: Merge into a new array of size m + n (O(m + n) space). Merging two sorted halves fully in place without a buffer is possible but much more complex.

followUps.question: How does this relate to merge sort?
followUps.answer: It is the merge step. Merge sort splits the array in halves recursively and merges them back, giving O(n log n).

questions.title: Sort Colors (Dutch National Flag)
questions.prompt:
An array `nums` contains only the values `0`, `1` and `2` (think red, white and blue). Sort it **in place** so that all 0s come first, then all 1s, then all 2s.

Do it in a single pass with O(1) extra space, without calling a library sort.
hints: Counting the 0s, 1s and 2s and rewriting the array works in two passes. Can you do it in one?
Keep three regions — 0s on the left, 2s on the right, 1s in the middle — plus an unknown part that shrinks.
Pointers `low`, `mid`, `high`. nums[mid] == 0 → swap with low, advance both; == 1 → mid++; == 2 → swap with high, high-- (do not advance mid).

approaches.name: Library sort
approaches.idea: Call the built-in sort.

approaches.name: Counting sort
approaches.idea: Count each value in one pass, rewrite the array in a second pass.

approaches.name: Dutch national flag
approaches.idea: Three pointers partition into 0s / 1s / unknown / 2s in one pass.

solution.summary: Dutch national flag: everything before `low` is 0, between `low` and `mid` is 1, after `high` is 2. Look at nums[mid]: a 0 is swapped to `low` and both advance; a 1 just advances `mid`; a 2 is swapped to `high` and `high` shrinks without moving `mid`. One pass, O(1) space.
solution.explanation:
**Regions (the invariant)**
- `nums[0 .. low−1]` = 0s
- `nums[low .. mid−1]` = 1s
- `nums[mid .. high]` = not examined yet
- `nums[high+1 .. n−1]` = 2s

**Algorithm.** While `mid ≤ high`, look at `nums[mid]`:
1. **0** → swap with `nums[low]`, then `low++` and `mid++`.
2. **1** → it already belongs to the middle block: `mid++`.
3. **2** → swap with `nums[high]`, then `high--`. Do **not** move `mid`: the value that came from `high` has not been examined.

The unknown region shrinks by one every iteration, so the loop runs exactly n times.

**Why advancing mid after a 0-swap is safe.** The value coming back from `low` is either a 1 (from the 1s block) or, when `low == mid`, the same 0. Either way it is already classified.

**Complexity.** O(n) time in one pass, O(1) extra space. This is Dijkstra's Dutch national flag partition — the same three-way partition that makes quicksort fast on arrays with many equal keys.

complexity.time: O(n) — the unknown region shrinks by one per iteration

keyPoints: Name the four regions and the invariant before coding
0 → swap with low, then low++ and mid++
2 → swap with high, then only high-- (the swapped-in value is unchecked)
Loop while mid <= high
One pass and O(1) space; counting sort is the simpler two-pass answer

visuals.title: Dutch national flag on nums = [1, 2, 0, 0, 2, 1, 0]
visuals.caption: Green bands are finished (0s left, 2s right), the blue band holds 1s, unmarked cells between mid and high are still unknown.

steps.note: Everything is unknown: `low = mid = 0`, `high = n − 1`. We grow a 0s block on the left, a 2s block on the right and a 1s block behind `mid`.
nums[mid] = 1 → already in the middle block; just `mid++`.
nums[mid] = 2 → swap with nums[high] to extend the 2s block; `high--`. `mid` stays because the value swapped in (0) is unchecked.
nums[mid] = 0 → swap with nums[low] (a 1) to extend the 0s block; `low++`, `mid++`.
nums[mid] = 0 → swap with nums[low] (a 1) to extend the 0s block; `low++`, `mid++`.
nums[mid] = 0 → swap with nums[low] (a 1) to extend the 0s block; `low++`, `mid++`.
nums[mid] = 2 → swap with nums[high] to extend the 2s block; `high--`. `mid` stays because the value swapped in (1) is unchecked.
nums[mid] = 1 → already in the middle block; just `mid++`.
`mid` (5) > `high` (4): no unknown cells remain → [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2], sorted in one pass.

visuals.title: Library sort vs counting sort vs Dutch national flag
rows: A small, known range of values
No — rewrites values from the counts
Yes — swaps (works for objects with a colour key)

pitfalls: Advancing `mid` after swapping with `high` — an unexamined 0 or 2 gets stuck in the middle
Looping while `mid < high`, which leaves the last unknown element unexamined
Offering counting sort when the interviewer explicitly asked for one pass

followUps.question: How would you sort k different colours?
followUps.answer: Counting sort in O(n + k) time and O(k) space; or, in place, partition recursively by colour ranges for O(n log k).

followUps.question: Where else is three-way partitioning used?
followUps.answer: In 3-way quicksort: partition into < pivot, == pivot and > pivot so equal keys are never recursed on — it turns the many-duplicates worst case into linear work.

quiz.question: Which property of the input makes the converging two-pointer search for a pair with a given sum correct?
quiz.explanation: Sorted order is what lets you discard numbers[left] when the sum is too small (only moving left can increase it) and numbers[right] when it is too big. Duplicates and negative values are fine.

quiz.question: In Container With Most Water, height[left] = 3 and height[right] = 8. Which pointer should move?
options: right, because it is the taller wall
left, because the shorter wall limits the area
Neither — stop and return the current area
quiz.explanation: Any container that keeps the wall of height 3 with a closer partner is narrower and still at most 3 high, so it cannot beat the current area. Discard the shorter wall: left++.

quiz.question: What is the overall time complexity of 3Sum using sorting plus two pointers?
quiz.explanation: Sorting is O(n log n); then each of n anchors runs an O(n) two-pointer scan, so O(n²) dominates.

quiz.question: In the Dutch national flag algorithm, nums[mid] is 2 and you swap it with nums[high]. What happens to the pointers?
quiz.explanation: The value swapped into mid came from the unexamined region, so it still has to be checked. Only the 2s block grows: high--. Advancing mid here is the classic bug.

quiz.question: Why does Merge Sorted Array fill nums1 from the back?
options: It is asymptotically faster than merging from the front
The free slots are at the end, so writing there never overwrites an unmerged nums1 value
Because nums2 has to be read in reverse order
quiz.explanation: Both directions take O(m + n). The point is safety: the placeholders are at the end, so placing the largest values there first never destroys a real value that is still needed — no buffer required.

quiz.question: removeDuplicates([0, 0, 1, 1, 2]) returns k = 3. What is guaranteed about nums afterwards?
options: nums[0..2] is [0, 1, 2]; the remaining slots can hold anything
nums is unchanged; only k is computed
quiz.explanation: Only the first k slots are specified. With the read/write solution the array is actually [0, 1, 2, 1, 2] — leftovers stay because the algorithm only overwrites slots and never truncates the array (a Java array cannot shrink at all).

quiz.question: In Trapping Rain Water, how much water stands above index i?
quiz.explanation: Water rises until it spills over the lower of the two tallest walls around i. Only looking at direct neighbours is wrong: a far-away tall wall can still hold water.

quiz.question: What extra space does the in-place two-pointer palindrome check use?
quiz.explanation: Only two indices are stored. Building a cleaned copy and reversing it would be O(n).

quiz.question: For Two Sum on an UNSORTED array where you must return the original indices, what is usually the best approach?
options: A one-pass hash map from value to index
Converging two pointers on the raw array
Sort the values, then return the two pointer positions
quiz.explanation: Two pointers need sorted order, and sorting loses the original indices unless you sort (value, index) pairs in O(n log n). A hash map gives O(n) time directly.

quiz.question: In 3Sum, why is `if (i > 0 && nums[i] === nums[i - 1]) continue;` correct while `if (nums[i] === nums[i + 1]) continue;` is wrong?
options: The first version misses triplets that repeat a value
The second version only risks an out-of-bounds read
The second version skips the first copy of a value, losing triplets like [-1, -1, 2]
quiz.explanation: Comparing with i + 1 makes the LAST copy the anchor, so the earlier copies can no longer serve as the second value. Comparing with i − 1 processes the first copy (later copies are still to its right) and only skips repeats.

quiz.question: In the two-pointer Trapping Rain Water solution, height[left] = 2 and height[right] = 5. Why can index left be settled right away?
options: Because left always moves before right
Because a wall of height ≥ 5 exists on the right, so leftMax (not the right side) limits the water at left
Because the water at the left edge is always 0
Because leftMax is reset to 0 at every step
quiz.explanation: water[left] = min(maxLeft, maxRight) − height[left]. The right side has a bar of at least 5 and every bar the left pointer passed was lower than something on the right, so maxRight ≥ leftMax and the minimum is leftMax.
